title: Trujillo to Cajamarca: the Swineherd Who Took an Empire
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Trujillo, the Base-born Son of Extremadura

stops.name: Trujillo, the castle above the plain
stops.campa: Under the granite castle of Trujillo, in the harsh table-land of Extremadura, Francisco is born to Captain Gonzalo Pizarro and a servant girl, Francisca González, out of wedlock and out of any house's notice. The chroniclers will later dispute the year (1471, 1475, 1478), as they dispute so much of him, but not the shame of his birth nor the indifference that follows it. No font records the day. He grows up in his father's shadow and his mother's poverty, one bastard among the many Extremadura will send across the Ocean to make himself a name by the sword alone.
suggested_refs: The equestrian statue of Pizarro, Plaza Mayor de Trujillo
The castle (alcázar) of Trujillo above the Extremadura plain

stops.name: Trujillo, the swineherd legend
stops.campa: He can neither read nor write; no one troubles to teach him. The tradition sets him to herding his father's (or another man's) swine on the stony commons outside the walls, so destitute, the story insists, that he is reduced like the prodigal son to eating the very swill thrown to the animals in his charge. It is a legend built to be outgrown: the same hands that cannot hold a pen will hold a sword well enough to unmake an empire, and the chroniclers who scorn the swineherd will not scorn the marqués he becomes.
suggested_refs: The swineherd legend of young Pizarro, retold in every popular life since the sixteenth century

stops.name: Seville, the gate to the Indies
stops.campa: He needs little encouragement to abandon the ignoble trade of the pigsty. Word runs through Extremadura of a New World across the Ocean where even base-born men win encomiendas and titles; his own kinsman's line, the Cortés of Medellín, will send another such son within the decade. Pizarro walks the short road down to Seville, city of the Casas de Contratación, of caravels loading for Hispaniola on the tide of the Guadalquivir, and takes service, a soldier with no name of his own, in the fleet that Governor Nicolás de Ovando is gathering for the Indies.
suggested_refs: The Torre del Oro and the Guadalquivir docks of Seville, gateway of the Carrera de Indias

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Ovando's fleet of thirty sail
stops.campa: Thirty ships and twenty-five hundred men clear the bar of the Guadalquivir at Sanlúcar under Governor Ovando, the largest fleet yet sent to the Indies: among them the unlettered Pizarro, one soldier among the crowd, and the young Bartolomé de las Casas, who will later write against everything this fleet is sailing to do. Christopher Columbus himself, on his fourth and last voyage, quits the same roadstead weeks after them, outbound for a coast neither man yet imagines they share. Pizarro's Ocean has begun.
suggested_refs: Sanlúcar de Barrameda's harbor bar, mouth of the Guadalquivir, departure point of the Carrera de Indias

stops.name: Santo Domingo, landfall among the first conquistadors
stops.campa: The fleet makes the harbor of Santo Domingo, capital of the Spanish Isle, where the same stone tower that will one day hold Columbus under arrest already stands above the Ozama. Pizarro steps ashore an anonymous soldier of fortune among hundreds like him, and spends the better part of a decade in the wars and repartimientos of Hispaniola and the pearl coast, learning the trade that will make him: how a handful of armored men break the will of a hundred unarmored ones, and how little the Crown asks of the manner of it.
suggested_refs: The Torre del Homenaje, Santo Domingo, shared pin with the Admiral's own landfalls and imprisonment
sources: columbus.journey.json, 'Santo Domingo, Bobadilla, and the irons' (shared site)

stops.name: Urabá, the doomed colony of San Sebastián
stops.campa: Under Alonso de Ojeda, Pizarro sails to the Gulf of Urabá to seed a colony on the Tierra Firme itself: San Sebastián, a stockade fort raised against hostile bowmen who dip their arrows in a poison that kills within the hour. Hunger and the poisoned shafts empty the garrison faster than any battle; Ojeda sails back to Hispaniola for relief and does not return. Pizarro is left in command of the survivors with orders to hold fifty days and no longer. He holds the ground until the ships of Enciso and Balboa find him, half the company already dead.
suggested_refs: The Gulf of Urabá, Colombia, cradle of the mainland's first Spanish footholds, San Sebastián's traditional site near modern Necoclí

stops.name: Santa María la Antigua del Darién, the first city of Tierra Firme
stops.campa: The survivors of San Sebastián cross the gulf with Balboa and found, on ground the Indians call Darién, the first permanent Spanish town of the American mainland: a stockade, a church, a plaza traced in the mud. Pizarro serves here as one of Balboa's captains through the campaigns that break the chiefs of the isthmus one after another: Cémaco, Careta, Ponca, learning the geography of Tierra Firme and the rumor, repeated by every cacique they plunder, of a sea beyond the mountains and a kingdom of gold still farther south.
suggested_refs: The archaeological park of Santa María la Antigua del Darién, Chocó, Colombia, first Spanish city on the mainland
sources: Wikipedia, 'Santa María la Antigua del Darién'

stops.name: The Sierra of Quarequa, the ascent to the South Sea
stops.campa: With a hundred and ninety Spaniards and a thousand native bearers, Balboa cuts south from Darién through jungle, swamp, and the cacique Quarequa's spears, and climbs the last bare ridge alone, ahead of the column, so that no other Christian eye takes the sight before his. Pizarro is among the hundred he has chosen for this march. At the top Balboa falls to his knees; behind him the company crowds up and falls to its knees also, and there below them, silver in the noon light, lies a sea no European has ever seen. They sing the Te Deum on the ridge.
suggested_refs: The ridge above the Gulf of San Miguel, Darién province, Panama, traditional site of the first sighting, 25 September 1513

stops.name: The Gulf of San Miguel, Balboa wades into the new ocean
stops.campa: Four days down from the ridge to the shingle, Balboa wades waist-deep into the tide with sword and banner and claims the South Sea, its islands, and every coast it washes for the Crown of Castile, in the hearing of Pizarro and the rest of the company drawn up on the strand. It is the discovery on which every later thing in this life depends: the sea that will one day carry three small ships south along an unmapped coast, past Tumbes, toward an empire richer than any cacique of the isthmus has yet described.
suggested_refs: The Gulf of San Miguel, where Balboa claimed the South Sea for Spain, 29 September 1513
sources: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Balboa Reaches the Pacific Ocean'

stops.name: Acla, the arrest of Balboa
stops.campa: Six years the discoverer of the South Sea and his rival governor Pedrarias Dávila circle each other with feigned marriages and real suspicion, until Pedrarias, believing new treason, sends orders to the fort of Acla. It is Pizarro, Balboa's own old comrade of the Darién marches, the man who knelt beside him on the ridge, who rides out and takes him under arrest without a blow struck, and delivers him to the judge who will condemn him. Loyalty to the governor who pays him outweighs the memory of the sea they discovered together; the ledger of this life keeps that kind of arithmetic from the start.
suggested_refs: The ruins of the fort of Acla, Caribbean coast of the Darién, Panama

stops.name: Panamá, the founding of the city, alcalde
stops.campa: On the Pacific shore Pedrarias founds the city of Panamá, hinge between the two seas and the last Spanish town before whatever lies south along the coast Balboa opened. Pizarro is granted land on the Chagres and, for his service against Balboa, the office of alcalde: mayor and magistrate of the new city, 1519 to 1523. It is respectability of a kind he has never had: a house, an encomienda, a chair on the cabildo. He is past forty and comfortable. The rumors of gold to the south, which he has heard for a decade, have not yet made him move.
suggested_refs: Panamá Viejo, ruins of the first city of Panamá, founded 1519

stops.name: Panamá, the Empresa of the Levant, the pact of three
stops.campa: In the church of the Mercedarians at Panamá, Pizarro signs the pact, the Empresa del Levante, with the soldier Diego de Almagro and the priest Hernando de Luque, who supplies what money there is. Each swears the enterprise to the south will be shared alike, gold, land, and rank, whoever bears the worse hardship. Pizarro is close to fifty, comfortable, an alcalde with land on the Chagres; he sets it all aside for a coast no European has sailed beyond the Gulf of San Miguel. Nothing in the rumor of gold has yet been seen by Christian eyes.
suggested_refs: The Empresa del Levante, 10 March 1524, the founding pact of the conquest of Peru

stops.name: Puerto de la Hambre, the first voyage's hunger
stops.campa: The first voyage south, a hundred and twelve men and a scatter of horses, crawls down an uncharted coast of mangrove and rain past Puerto Piñas and the Colombian rivers, and comes at last to a bay of driven famine the company names, without irony, Puerto de la Hambre: the Port of Hunger. Provisions fail; the relief ship does not come; men eat shellfish, roots, the flesh of their own dead. More than twenty starve outright. Pizarro holds the survivors together on this shore by will alone, waiting on a ship that is late by months, not days.
suggested_refs: The Colombian Pacific coast near the mouth of the Río San Juan, traditional site of Puerto de la Hambre
sources: Studocu, 'Resumen de los Viajes de Pizarro a Perú'

stops.name: Isla del Gallo, the line in the sand, the Thirteen of Fame
stops.campa: Marooned on this mangrove islet while Almagro begs reinforcements in Panamá, the company mutinies against another season of hunger and fever. The relief ship of Governor Ríos comes not with men but an order home. Pizarro draws a single line in the wet sand with the point of his sword, and turns to face them: on that side, Panamá, and poverty; on this side, the south, and what it holds. He steps across his own line first. Thirteen men, the Thirteen of Fame, cross after him. The rest sail home to safety and the tradition's contempt.
stops.quote: There lies Peru with its riches; here, Panamá and its poverty. Choose, each man, what best becomes a brave Castilian. For my part, I go to the south.
stops.quote_source: Attributed by tradition (Gómara, Historia General de las Indias; Zárate; popularized in Prescott, History of the Conquest of Peru, 1847)
suggested_refs: The line in the sand of Isla del Gallo, the founding image of the Famous Thirteen (Los Trece de la Fama)
sources: Adventures in Historyland, 'The Line in the Sand'

stops.name: Tumbes, the first sight of the empire
stops.campa: The pilot Bartolomé Ruiz, sailing on ahead, has already taken a balsa raft of Tumbes traders off the coast: cotton cloth, worked silver, gold ornaments, emeralds, proof at last that the rumor was true. Now Pizarro's own remaining company sails into the bay of Tumbes and finds a stone-built town of terraced fields, canals, a fortress and a temple of the Sun, subjects of a lord called the Inca whose empire, the Tumbes people say, runs the length of the mountains to the south. Thirteen starving men have found, at last, the kingdom the whole voyage was staked on.
suggested_refs: The bay of Tumbes, first Inca province seen by Europeans, and Bartolomé Ruiz's captured balsa raft
sources: World History Encyclopedia, 'Pizarro & the Fall of the Inca Empire'

stops.name: Toledo, the Capitulación, before the absent Emperor
stops.campa: Pizarro crosses the Ocean again, this time to the Emperor's own court, to lay Tumbes and the balsa's gold before Charles V. The Emperor is elsewhere; the Empress Isabella signs in Toledo the Capitulación that makes Pizarro governor, captain general, adelantado for life of New Castile, the two hundred leagues of coast from the Santiago River to Chincha, with a knighthood of Santiago besides. Almagro, his partner of five years' hunger, receives the lesser governorship of Tumbes alone; Luque is named bishop. The document that will conquer an empire also plants, in its unequal shares, the seed of a civil war.
suggested_refs: The Capitulación de Toledo, 26 July 1529, the royal charter of the conquest of Peru
sources: Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes, 'Real Cédula... Capitulación'

stops.name: Trujillo, recruiting the brothers of his blood
stops.campa: Before sailing back he returns once more to Trujillo, the town that never troubled to know him as a boy, and gathers to the enterprise the men of his own blood: his half-brothers Hernando, Juan, and Gonzalo Pizarro, and his half-brother by another line, Francisco Martín de Alcántara. Extremadura sends four brothers across the Ocean on the strength of one bastard's royal grant, the same soil that will one day send Hernán Cortés's own kin, and the tradition binds the two conquerors as cousins of a single hard country. All four will die in Peru; none of natural causes.
suggested_refs: The house of the Pizarro brothers, Trujillo, cross-referenced with the Extremadura kinship tradition shared with Hernán Cortés

stops.name: Nombre de Dios, landfall from Spain, the quarrel with Almagro
stops.campa: Returning from Spain with his royal patents and his brothers, Pizarro makes landfall at Nombre de Dios, the Caribbean door of the isthmus, where Almagro comes hurrying to meet him, and finds the pact of equal thirds signed away at Toledo: governor, captain general, adelantado, all of it Pizarro's, and for himself only Tumbes. The quarrel flares hot on the very beach; Almagro must be talked back into the enterprise with promises of titles still unwon. The partnership survives its first wound. It will not survive the empire the wound is carried into.
suggested_refs: Nombre de Dios, Caribbean terminus of the Camino Real across the isthmus of Panamá
sources: IFEA, 'Francisco Pizarro, La larga preparación del asalto (1528-1532)'

stops.name: Panamá, the banners blessed, the third fleet sails
stops.campa: In the church of La Merced at Panamá, the same Mercedarian church where the pact of three was sworn six years before, the expedition hears mass and has its banners blessed on the feast-heavy end of December, 1530. In the first days of January the three ships stand out from the Pacific port at last: about a hundred and eighty men, a few dozen horses, the Pizarro brothers all aboard, Almagro left behind once more to raise reinforcements and follow. It is the third sailing south, and the one the Capitulación has armed with an empire's paper title.
suggested_refs: The church of La Merced, Panamá Viejo, where the banners of the third expedition were blessed, 27 December 1530
sources: IFEA, 'Francisco Pizarro, La larga preparación del asalto (1528-1532)'

stops.name: San Miguel de Tangarará, the first Spanish town in Peru
stops.campa: On the banks of the Chira, Pizarro founds San Miguel: the third Spanish city of South America and the first in Peru, a cabildo, a church, a garrison of the halt and the sick left behind when the main column marches inland. He has landed already into a kingdom split by civil war: the emperor Huáscar defeated and held by his half-brother Atahualpa, whose armies have not yet turned to notice the hundred and sixty foreigners now walking, on foot and on unfamiliar horses, straight toward the high sierra where Atahualpa camps with his court.
suggested_refs: Tangarará, on the right bank of the Chira, Marcavelica district, Sullana, founding site of San Miguel, the first Spanish city in Peru (the town later moved to Piura la Vieja, La Matanza)

segments.name: Cajamarca, the Ambush and the Ransom

stops.name: Cajamarca, the envoys at Atahualpa's baths
stops.campa: The column of a hundred and sixty enters the empty city of Cajamarca and finds the Inca's army, tens of thousands strong, encamped in tents on the hillside above, at the hot springs where Atahualpa is taking his ease after the defeat of Huáscar. Hernando de Soto and then Hernando Pizarro ride out to the camp, deliver Francisco's invitation to a meeting in the plaza, and return awed by what they have seen: an army beyond counting, and an Inca who receives armed strangers on horseback without rising from his golden stool.
suggested_refs: The Baños del Inca outside Cajamarca, where Atahualpa's camp lay before the ambush
sources: World History Encyclopedia, 'Pizarro & the Fall of the Inca Empire'

stops.name: Cajamarca, the ambush in the plaza, Atahualpa seized
stops.campa: Atahualpa enters the great plaza at dusk on a litter of gold, borne by his lords, with several thousand unarmed attendants singing before him. Friar Vicente de Valverde comes out with cross and missal and calls on him to accept the faith and the Emperor; Atahualpa turns the book in his hands, finds it dumb, and throws it to the ground. At the signal a cannon fires and the cry of Santiago goes up from every doorway; cavalry and gunfire break into the unarmed crowd, and in less than an hour thousands lie dead in the plaza. Pizarro himself, sword drawn, seizes Atahualpa from his fallen litter and takes him prisoner with his own hand.
stops.quote: And if you were taken prisoner, and your people defeated and killed, it was because you came with so great an army against us, when we came to ask that you come in peace — and you threw to the ground the book in which are the words of God; for this our Lord permitted that your pride be brought low.
stops.quote_source: Francisco de Xérez, secretary to Pizarro, Verdadera relación de la conquista del Perú (1534)
suggested_refs: The Plaza de Armas de Cajamarca, site of the ambush, 16 November 1532

stops.name: Cajamarca, the ransom promised, a room to be filled
stops.campa: From his captivity Atahualpa offers his own price for freedom: he will fill the long chamber where he is held with gold as high as a man can reach on the wall, and two smaller adjoining rooms with silver, twice over. Runners go out from Cajamarca to every shrine and palace of the empire; llama trains begin arriving from Cusco with plate stripped from the Coricancha itself. Pizarro accepts the bargain and waits, months on end, while the greatest ransom in the history of the world accumulates, plank by golden plank, inside the room the Inca measured with his own raised hand.
suggested_refs: El Cuarto del Rescate (the Ransom Chamber), the surviving Inca stone building at Cajamarca
sources: History Collection, 'Atahualpa: The Last Inca Emperor'

stops.name: Cajamarca, the room filled once with gold
stops.campa: By late spring the chamber stands filled to the mark Atahualpa set with his own hand: plate, vessels, idols, and ornament of gold from every temple of the empire, weighed and melted down by the royal smiths under guard. It is, the chroniclers agree, the richest single ransom ever paid on earth: some six thousand pounds of gold delivered for the freedom of one man. Pizarro sets aside the royal fifth for the Crown and divides the rest among the company by rank, from the horsemen down to the sick left behind at San Miguel, who each still draw a share.
suggested_refs: The gold ransom of Atahualpa, distributed at Cajamarca, 1533, the richest single ransom in recorded history
sources: SA Expeditions, 'Atahualpa is captured by Pizarro at Cajamarca'

stops.name: Cajamarca, the rooms filled twice with silver
stops.campa: The silver follows, twice the promised measure, hauled down from Cusco and the mining camps of the sierra on the backs of thousands of llamas driven by subjects who still, in these weeks, obey their captive Inca's word before any Spaniard's. Between gold and silver the company divides some twenty-four tons of treasure: an empire's temple-wealth converted, plank and idol and drinking-vessel alike, into the coin and plate of Castile. Atahualpa has kept his word to the letter. It buys him not one further day of the freedom he bargained for.
suggested_refs: The silver ransom of Atahualpa, completed 1533, delivered from Cusco and the sierra mines

stops.name: Cajamarca, the trial and the garrote of the Inca
stops.campa: Charged before a hastily convened court with idolatry, the murder of his brother Huáscar, and plotting an army against his captors, the last charge got up out of rumor and fear, Atahualpa is condemned to burn. Friar Valverde offers him baptism to buy a mercy: the rope instead of the flame. He accepts, takes the name Francisco after his captor, and is garroted the same night in the plaza where he was seized eight months before. Pizarro, some chroniclers record, mourns him after the fact and wears black; the mourning changes nothing that the gold has already bought.
suggested_refs: The Plaza de Armas de Cajamarca, site of both the seizure and the execution of Atahualpa, 26 July 1533
sources: History Collection, 'Atahualpa: The Last Inca Emperor'

segments.name: Cusco and the Founding of Lima

stops.name: Jauja, the first camp of the march
stops.campa: The column marches up out of Cajamarca along the Inca royal road, through passes and rope bridges built for llama trains, not horses, and makes its first extended camp in the fertile valley of Jauja, high, cold, and rich with maize terraces. Pizarro leaves a garrison and the sick here under Riquelme with the still-unassayed remainder of the treasure, and considers, briefly, founding his capital on this very plain before the lowland coast is even known to him. Ahead lies Cusco, and General Quisquis's army, still loyal to the dead Atahualpa's cause, falling back before them into the sierra.
suggested_refs: Jauja, first Spanish administrative camp of the march to Cusco
sources: Wikipedia, 'Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire'
World History Encyclopedia, 'Pizarro & the Fall of the Inca Empire'

stops.name: Cusco, entry into the navel of the world
stops.campa: Pizarro rides into Huacaypata, the great plaza of Cusco, Qosqo, the navel of the world, at the head of a column too small, by any ordinary reckoning, to have taken an empire ten thousand miles long. The city falls without a battle: General Quisquis has already withdrawn north, and the survivor prince Manco Inca, spared his brother's massacre, rides in at Pizarro's side, ready to be crowned as the puppet who will keep the provinces quiet a little longer. The stones of the Coricancha, still sheathed in gold, wait a day's grace before the stripping begins.
suggested_refs: The Plaza de Armas of Cusco (Huacaypata), heart of the Inca capital and, in time, the colonial one, cross-referenced for the plaza constellation of essay 207 and San Cristóbal above the city
sources: historyng.com, 'Francisco Pizarro Captures the Inca Capital of Cusco'

stops.name: Cusco, the Coricancha stripped, Manco Inca crowned
stops.campa: The Coricancha, temple of the Sun, is stripped of its golden sheeting, its garden of golden maize, the mummies of dead emperors robbed of the ornament they were dressed in for their long death-in-life. Days later, on the sixteenth of December, Pizarro sets the fringe of royal office on Manco Inca's brow in the plaza below and names him Sapa Inca under the Emperor Charles: a coronation staged to hold the empire's obedience through a Spanish mouth. Manco will wear the crown ten years, three in outward peace, before the rope of that same borrowed sovereignty snaps.
suggested_refs: The Coricancha, temple of the Sun, over which the church of Santo Domingo now stands in Cusco

stops.name: Lima, Ciudad de los Reyes founded
stops.campa: Cusco, high and landlocked, cannot serve a governor who must answer to Seville by ship. Pizarro rejects Jauja too and rides down to the green valley of the Rímac, near the sea and its own good river, and on the eighteenth of January, near the feast of the Three Kings, traces with his own hand the grid of streets and the plaza mayor of a new capital, named Ciudad de los Reyes, the City of Kings, though history will keep the older Quechua name, Lima, for the river that waters it. It will outlive every other stone he lays.
suggested_refs: The Plaza Mayor of Lima, laid out by Pizarro 18 January 1535, still the city's civic heart

stops.name: Cusco, Almagro returns from Chile, the city seized
stops.campa: Almagro, the ransomed partner of the pact of three, comes back exhausted and empty-handed from a ruinous expedition into the deserts of Chile to find that Cusco, which he believes his own by the letter of a rival grant from the Crown, has been claimed instead for the Pizarros. He raises the men of his broken expedition, marches on the city while Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro hold it for their brother, and takes it by force, imprisoning both. Two Extremaduran captains of the same conquering enterprise now hold the same capital at each other's throats.
suggested_refs: Cusco, contested capital of the Pizarro-Almagro civil war, 1537-38

stops.name: Las Salinas, the battle for Cusco
stops.campa: On the white salt flats southeast of Cusco, Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro's army meets Almagro's in the open, cavalry charging across ground bare and firm in the April dry season. Rodrigo Orgóñez, Almagro's field commander, is killed in the first hour; Almagro himself, too weak with illness to fight from the saddle, is taken from his litter. Francisco Pizarro, who has stayed at Lima through the whole civil quarrel, receives the news of the victory his brothers have won for him over the ransomed partner who once staked his own fortune to send four brothers across an ocean.
suggested_refs: The salt flats of Las Salinas, southeast of Cusco, 13°34'S 71°59'W, site of the decisive battle

stops.name: Cusco, the garrote of Almagro
stops.campa: Old and broken in his cell, Almagro is tried, condemned, and garroted on Hernando Pizarro's order. Francisco does not countermand it, and history will not let him disclaim it. Almagro is then beheaded, his head set up in the plaza he once seized by force, a warning to any partner who mistakes friendship for a fixed share of an empire. The pact of three signed in a Panamá church fourteen years before ends here, one signer dead by the rope, another soon to answer for it with his own blood, the third, Luque, already some years in his grave.
suggested_refs: The Plaza de Armas of Cusco, site of Almagro's execution and public display, 8 July 1538

stops.name: Lima, the palace, the cross of blood
stops.campa: Twenty armed Almagristas, avenging the father's garrote on the son's behalf, storm Pizarro's palace on the plaza after Sunday dinner. Most of his guests flee down the stairs; his half-brother Martín de Alcántara and a handful of servants fight and die at the door while the old governor, past sixty, struggles to buckle on his breastplate too late. He kills two attackers and runs a third through before exhaustion and a sword-thrust to the throat bring him down. Falling, he draws a cross on the floor in his own blood, kisses it, and dies crying the one word: Jesús.
stops.quote_source: Agustín de Zárate, Historia del descubrimiento y conquista del Perú (1555), on Pizarro's last cry
suggested_refs: The site of Pizarro's palace on the Plaza Mayor of Lima, now the Government Palace of Peru
sources: History.com, 'Francisco Pizarro, conqueror of the Incas, assassinated'
InsideHook, 'The Epic Sword Fight That Finally Killed Pizarro'

stops.name: Lima, burial amid the city he founded
stops.campa: The city he traced six years before with his own hand buries him in haste and fear, the Almagrista faction now ruling the plaza he founded, his loyal friends scattered or in hiding. He is laid, the tradition says, wrapped in a cloak and interred without ceremony in the cathedral he had begun to raise on the same square: the marqués of an empire, murdered in his own hall by the sons of the partner his brothers had garroted, given the burial of a man nobody now dares to mourn aloud.
suggested_refs: The Cathedral of Lima, built on the site Pizarro assigned it in his 1535 plan of the city
sources: Medium, 'Pizarro's Tomb at the Cathedral of Lima'

stops.name: Lima Cathedral, the skull in the crypt, the false glass coffin
stops.campa: For eighty-six years, since 1891, a body identified as Pizarro's has lain on public view in a glass-sided coffin in the cathedral, embalmed and displayed for the pious and the curious alike. In 1977, workmen cleaning a forgotten crypt beneath the cathedral floor uncover a lead box inscribed: here is the skull of the Marquis Don Francisco Pizarro, who discovered and won Peru, and placed it under the crown of Castile, alongside a second box holding a jumble of other bones, dismembered like a relic long fought over. The glass coffin's occupant, it now seems certain, is someone else entirely.
suggested_refs: The inscribed lead box discovered in the crypt of Lima Cathedral, 1977
The glass-sided coffin displayed since 1891, since shown to hold the wrong remains
sources: Ancient Origins, 'Finding Francisco Pizarro: The Strange Story of Pizarro's Remains'
Strange Remains, 'The game of thrones written in bone, conquistador edition'

stops.name: Lima Cathedral, the true bones restored to the crypt
stops.campa: Forensic study at the University of Missouri, matching the skull's fractures against the throat-and-skull wounds the sixteenth-century chroniclers recorded of his death, confirms in 1984 what the lead inscription already claimed: these are the true bones of Francisco Pizarro. On the twenty-sixth of January 1985, four hundred and forty-four years after the Almagristas' swords found him, the real marqués is installed at last in a proper crypt of the cathedral he began, while the glass coffin that held a stranger for nearly a century is quietly emptied of its long, mistaken vigil.
suggested_refs: The crypt of Lima Cathedral, final and forensically confirmed resting place of Francisco Pizarro since January 1985
sources: UPI Archives, 'Several bones of Spanish explorer Francisco Pizarro recently matched'
Latin America Confidential, 'Unearthing a Conquistador's 500-Year-Old Mystery'
